With this revised manuscript the authors have addressed a number of my previous comments.  In particular, the methodology is now much more clearly described, and the software is easy to install via conda.  However, a few of my prior comments were not sufficiently addressed and the revisions have raised new questions.

Major comments:

1. The revised introduction does a better job of calling out the key assumption/limitation of NIFFLR, which is that all possible exons are known and provided to the tool.  However, a critical statement that justifies NIFFLR's approach is not sufficiently supported: "the primary use cases for NIFFLR are genomes with high-quality annotations, such as genomes of human, mouse, and other model organisms, where almost all exons have been discovered, and alternative isoforms are, in most cases, different combinations of the existing exons."  The authors should provide a citation that supports this claim or provide their own analysis of a real dataset that demonstrates that, in well-studied genomes, novel isoforms more often result from combinations of annotated exons than from novel exons (including small deviations of known exons).

2. Surely the assumption mentioned in #1 does not completely hold except in simulations and thus it is important that experiments be done to show how NIFFLR's performance is affected by the presence of novel exons, even if rare.  The authors' response seemed to suggest that the new SIRV analysis somewhat addresses this issue in that some of the SIRV exons are highly similar, but it is not clear in this case whether NIFFLR was provided with all possible SIRV exons as input - if so, then this is not a scenario involving novel exons.

3. The new scatterplots (Supplemental Figures S2-S6) are a welcome addition and informative.  However, the Pearson correlations given look too high given the plots.  I suspect Pearson correlations were calculated on raw counts, which span many orders of magnitude.  In this case it would be more informative to calculate Pearson correlation on log2(count + 1) values (as are displayed in the plot) or to use Spearman correlation.

Minor comments:

4. Although the method is much better described, the algorithm used to find the path that minimizes the penalty function is not specified.  I assume some sort of shortest path dynamic programming algorithm is used, but this should be specified to be complete.

5. The authors' response mentioned a script for testing NIFFLR using the SIRV E2 data.  I could not find this script after installing, nor is it mentioned in the README.

Partly

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

Although the authors added more evaluations, including a comparison of NIFFLR with Bambu and with other existing methods on SIRV transcript detection, the results didn’t demonstrate any significant advantages of NIFFLR.

Comments on authors’ response:

1. To me, “constructing transcripts from existing exons guided by long reads” does not constitute novelty. All of the methods that the authors tested were designed to identify transcripts based on long reads, and they performed better with more annotated exons. The statement here, “any exon shorter than this value will not be detected” may result in transcripts being unable to be detected that can be detected by other methods.

2. “Evaluating or comparing alignment methods was not the focus of our study”, but evaluating whether psa_aligner is the most suitable aligner for NIFFLR to identify and quantify transcript isoforms should be the focus of this study.

3. Although I have not tried it myself, releasing a new version of NIFFLR is appropriate to solve the bugs.

4. While simulated data can be used to test NIFFLR, they only provide very weak evidence due to limitations and biases. As I mentioned in the previous comments, SIRV data provide reliable ground truth for real long-read RNA-seq data and are much more useful for evaluation of discovery and quantification.

5. As shown in Table 2, NIFFLR has the same sensitivity but much lower precision than ESPRESSO. In fact, NIFFLR is one of the two least precise methods of the five. As I suggested in the previous comments, quantification should also be evaluated based on SIRV.

6. No matter how many previous papers the authors cited for using short-read data to quantify isoforms, they cannot justify evaluating long-read quantification using short-read data. Quantification from short-read data is not the ground truth. Instead, the authors can use SIRV, as mentioned above.

7. The authors’ response did not prove that ESPRESSO has a limited ability to discover novel isoforms, nor that NIFFLR is more capable of doing so than ESPRESSO. On the contrary, NIFFLR cannot discover novel isoforms with any novel splice donors or acceptors, which limits its ability to discover novel isoforms. The authors can randomly mask half or more of the annotated isoforms in SIRV to evaluate the sensitivity of ESPRESSO and NIFFLR.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to state that I do not consider it to be of an acceptable scientific standard, for reasons outlined above.

The paper tackles an interesting problem. However, the novelty is limited: the proposed method is a straightforward combination of two existing techniques. The writing is also difficult to follow in Sections 3-4, with undefined notation. On the positive side, the experimental evaluation is thorough, covering five datasets with proper ablations.

The reviewers submit a revised version of the NIFFLR manuscript, in particular expanding on the benchmarking by adding more tools as comparison and adding a section benchmarking SIRV detection, as well as greatly expanding the methods. These expanded sections greatly improve the interpretability of the work. However, I do not feel that several of my principal concerns were adequately addressed and I encourage the authors to respond to the following points to really communicate to the community what the precise use cases and limitations for NIFFLR are.

Major concerns:

1.

I understand the authors do not wish to support novel exon discovery. I think this is fine but the manuscript needs further text and analyses to make this limitation abundantly clear.

Currently, they state that NIFFLR would be useful in organisms where “nearly all exons have been discovered and alternative isoforms are, in most cases, different combinations of the existing exons”.

However, I find this statement to be a misrepresentation even for the most well-annotated organisms, based both on the literature and personal work with long-read RNA-seq data. From my own experience working with long read RNA-seq in human, still a substantial proportion of novel isoforms derive from “novel exons” (~ novel not in catalog transcripts; [Ref 1, Ref 2]), despite the fact that humans are highly-sequenced and well-annotated. At the very least the authors need to find and cite sources that support this claim because I am, as it stands, skeptical.

2. Related to point 1, the limitations of only considering annotated exons must be quantitatively assessed. The current simulation strategy does not assess this in any capacity.

As I previously suggested, the easiest way the reviewers can do this is use the simulation data from LRGASP that’s already been produced which includes novel transcripts of all types (NNC and NIC transcripts), and determine what percentage of transcript novelty they are missing because they exclude NNCs. Here’s the link: 
                https://cgl.gi.ucsc.edu/data/LRGASP/data/simulation/human_simulation/.

Minor concerns:

1. The text from the results section describing the plots in great detail should be instead moved to the legends.

2. The figures and legends could be improved for clarity. For instance, where the authors say “Box and whiskers show that NIFFLR has a tighter distribution than FLAIR, Bambu and ESPRESSO, though it is slightly outperformed by IsoQuant”, they might consider using and comparing statistics such as mean and variance / standard deviation to describe these trends instead of eyeballing the numbers from several boxplots which all look relatively uniform.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to state that I do not consider it to be of an acceptable scientific standard, for reasons outlined above.

Guo et al. proposed NIFFLR, a tool for assembling and quantifying transcripts using long-read RNA-seq data. However, the current manuscript does not provide sufficient evidence to demonstrate the novelty or efficiency of NIFFLR in analyzing long-read data. Their evaluation and conclusions are not convincing.

1 Most readers would be confused about the novelty or advances of NIFFLR. It’s based on the alignment of constructed exon-exon junction sequences, a strategy used by many tools long ago. Does this strategy work for mini-exons that are shorter than 10 nt or 20 nt? This strategy also heavily depends on annotated exons. Can it identify any novel splice donors or acceptors? For tissues or organisms with incomplete annotation, how will this strategy be affected? All of above need be carefully evaluated and described in details.

2 The aligner (psa_aligner) used by the authors needs comprehensively assessment, e.g. whether psa_aligner is suitable for noisy long-read data. An evaluation and comparison with the commonly used long-read aligner Minimap2 should be included.

3 The NIFFLR programming script is poorly written and difficult to install and use for analysis. For example, when I tried to run NIFFLR, I received an error message from python (not NIFFLR) and could not finished the analysis. The error, “IndexError: list index out of range”, occurred during the “performing filtering and quantification” step.

4 The authors used simulated data to evaluate NIFFLR and other tools. However, this evaluation may result in biased results. Many reports have noted that existing simulators are not suitable for evaluation. For example, according to a recent paper published by Dr. Hagen Tilgner and colleagues (Mikheenko A, et al., 2022 [Ref 1]), NanoSim randomly selects a starting position in a transcript to simulate truncation based on a uniform distribution. However, in real long-read data, a uniform distribution cannot be observed.

5 A direct comparison of the tools for transcript identification and quantification using real long-read data with ground truth need be included. Many previous studies used SIRV E2 for evaluation, which contains 69 synthesized transcript isoforms with different abundances. I actually tried to run NIFFLR to analyze SIRV data, but it failed. NIFFLR produced an "exon extraction failed" error when processing the GTF annotation of SIRV, while I did not encounter any errors when using other tools. This is another example of poor programming of NIFFLR.

6 I am stunned that the authors used transcript abundance from short-read data to evaluate the performance of long-read tools. The bias of short-read data has been so widely reported. For example, a Nature Methods paper published by Chen et al. 2025 [Ref 2] provided important evidence on this. In addition to the bias, the novel transcript isoforms in the data that are similar to annotated isoforms would also confuse short-read quantification.

7 The authors need to provide sufficient evidence before arbitrarily judging existing tools. For example, they described ESPRESSO’s strategy for identifying novel splice junctions as “a stringent criterion that limits its ability to discover novel junctions”. However, they did not provide any evidence regarding the sensitivity of detecting novel splice junctions. Novel splice junctions can be further divided into junctions with novel splice sites and junctions as novel combination of annotated splice sites. Both types need to be compared between ESPRESSO and NIFFLR before the authors can draw such a conclusion.

8 Why was BamBu (Chen Y, et al., 2023 [Ref 3]) not included in the evaluation and comparison? BamBu was published online more than two years ago and has been widely used for long-read data analysis. To demonstrate the advantages of their tool, the authors will need to compare it with BamBu.

The authors describe a novel method and associated software, NIFFLR, for identifying and quantifying expressed transcript structures (both known and novel) from long, noisy RNA sequencing data, such as that produced by Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT).  A key challenge for methods addressing this task is the difficulty in identifying the precise locations of exon boundaries in the presence of frequent sequencing errors, particularly indels.  The novel approach taken by NIFFLR is the converse of that of other methods: instead of aligning reads to the genome, NIFFLR aligns annotated exons within the genome to the read.   NIFFLR uses a partial suffix array approach to efficiently align exons to the reads and a graph-based algorithm to identify the likely transcript structure for each read, followed by a series of heuristics to filter and quantify the transcripts.  With both simulated and real data, NIFFLR's accuracy is compared to that of three other methods: FLAIR2, IsoQuant, and ESPRESSO.  These experiments suggest that NIFFLR has high sensitivity and quantification accuracy comparable to the next best method.  Runtime measurements show that NIFFLR runs in time comparable to the fastest methods.

Major comments:

1. A key limitation of the method is its reliance on a known set of exons: all predicted transcripts must be combinations of known exons.  It appears that even slight variations in the boundaries of exons must be previously annotated for the method to predict transcripts with those variant exons. This general issue is brought up in the last two sentences of the discussion.  The authors suggest that when the full exon set is not known, short read data could be used to delineate the exons.  That may be a feasible strategy, but it is not implemented or evaluated in this work, nor do the evaluations consider novel exons.  This work would be strengthened by evaluations that include the more realistic scenario of novel exons (including 5' and 3' end variants of known exons).  By definition, NIFFLR will not be able to detect or quantify transcripts including these exons, but the impact of these exons on the precision and quantification accuracy of other transcripts should be measured.  Alternatively, the authors could implement the exon delineation strategy that they mentioned and examine NIFFLR's performance in combination with this strategy.  Admittedly, the evaluation on the real data set potentially includes reads from transcripts with novel exons, but it is difficult to discern from the results presented how any novel exons impacted the method's performance.

2. A number of details of the method are omitted or unclear.  A more formal and detailed presentation of the algorithm is needed.  For example, (A) what algorithm is used to solve the "exon tiling problem"? (B) what, precisely, is the objective function? (C) is the algorithm guaranteed to find the optimal solution? (D) how is an edge allowed between overlapping exons? (E) what is the intuition behind distributing reads "proportionally to the size of the container transcripts"?  Personally, I would like to see a more mathematical presentation and a figure depicting the steps of the entire procedure, particularly those detailed in the paragraph beginning "By design, all intron junctions...".

3. With respect to the software package, I was ultimately able to compile the software after installing the Boost and zlib development libraries.  It would be helpful to have these compilation dependencies noted in the README.  For ease of use by the community, it would also be helpful to have the package available via conda and/or Docker.  Finally, please provide a small test dataset with the software such that users can make sure that their installation is working and can see what the inputs and outputs look like.

Minor comments:

4. From the filtering steps of the algorithm, could there be an output provided that might indicate the presence of novel exons at a given locus?  For example, could the user be provided the number of reads that mapped to a locus but that were not ultimately assigned to a transcript?

5. For quantification evaluations, the box and whisker plots of log2 fold changes are helpful, but I would have also liked to have seen scatterplots of true vs. predicted counts (on log-scaled axes) along with correlation values, as has been common for short-read quantification methods.  Such scatterplots help to visualize potential subsets of transcripts that have biased predictions and trends relative to the magnitude of expression.

The author found that salivary HLA-DR4 levels were significantly lower in patient groups compared with healthy controls, whereas salivary MMP-8 and ACPA levels were significantly elevated in

Bama Andika Putra’s article reviews how the ASEAN nations have used telehealth to respond to COVID-19 and suggests regional policy solutions to address gaps in readiness for the digital age. The author finds that while COVID-19 has catalyzed telehealth across Southeast Asia with some success, it has also exposed deep disparities in the region and within the group of ASEAN nations which must be bridged going forward if telehealth is to remain sustainable in the long run. The article recommends exactly how to sustain the ASEAN processes while bridging those gaps. The author suggests that two types of major regional policy offer have the potential to close the gap: first, the ASEAN framework must be used to build telehealth as a shared responsibility within and beyond the organization by sharing national digital health blueprints through ASEAN facilitation and joint dialogue between ASEAN and “ASEAN Plus” members to align cyber law and standards, cybersecurity. The author stresses multiple times that all of this activity is still within the “ASEAN Way,” and no deviations from the member state are pushed. In the conclusions, the author openly admits that they even suggest if it would make sense to hold back commitments based on impactful capacity and willingness levels, or to worry about privacy or possible authoritarian system misuse, but then re-frames this situation in the conclusions. In the implications and recommendations, the author ultimately recommends a moderate approach to applying the framework among all states at their own pace, with privacy safeguards if referred to: the balance among urgent digital health implementation and the narrowing access to significantly for digital measures should remain the same.
